name: The Balassa–Samuelson Effect
statement: Consumer prices tend to be systematically higher in more productive, developed countries because productivity gaps in tradable goods push up wages and prices in non-tradable services.
statementAccent: productivity gaps in tradable goods push up wages and prices in non-tradable services
meaning: The effect explains why price levels, once adjusted for exchange rates, are systematically higher in richer countries than in poorer ones: a pattern also called the "Penn effect." It attributes this to cross-country productivity differences that are much larger in tradable sectors like manufacturing than in non-tradable sectors like local services.
mechanism: In wealthy countries, tradable-sector workers are far more productive than their counterparts in poor countries, which raises their wages. Because labour can move between sectors within a country, wages in the non-tradable sector rise to match even though non-tradable productivity has not improved. This pushes up the price of non-tradable goods and services, raising the overall domestic price level relative to lower-productivity countries.

examples.text: A haircut or fast-food meal costs far more in Zürich than in a developing-country capital, even though the service and the worker’s productivity are essentially identical, because Zürich wages are set by highly productive tradable sectors like finance.
Prices for the same non-tradable service, such as a pint of beer, tend to be higher in richer regions of a country, reflecting local wage differences driven by tradable-sector productivity.

Béla Balassa’s original 1964 paper was motivated by post-war European data showing recovering economies had different price levels and productivity growth rates that existing purchasing-power-parity theory could not explain.

whyItMatters: It is central to international economics because it shows why simple purchasing-power-parity comparisons overstate the real income gap between rich and poor countries, and it informs debates about currency undervaluation, real exchange-rate trends, and convergence.
limits: Empirical testing has produced mixed results across countries and periods; alternative or complementary explanations include distribution-sector productivity, capital-labour endowments, capital inflows ("Dutch disease"), trade barriers, and income-elastic demand for services, so productivity differentials alone often do not fully account for observed gaps.
misreadings: The effect is sometimes mistaken for a claim that developing countries have "artificially" cheap currencies; in fact it describes an equilibrium result of productivity differences between sectors, not a market distortion requiring correction.
origin: Independently proposed in 1964 by Hungarian-American economist Béla Balassa and American economist Paul Samuelson; a similar idea was hypothesised earlier by Roy Harrod in 1939 but was not widely recognised then.

sources.text: Balassa–Samuelson effect, Wikipedia. — the independent 1964 origin, the tradable/non-tradable productivity mechanism, and Harrod’s earlier 1939 hypothesis.
Béla Balassa, Wikipedia. — his 1964 Journal of Political Economy paper and role in developing the effect.
